source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, View on the Erie Canal (1832), public domain
stem: Which of the following best explains why the canal in the image mattered more to the growth of New York City than to the growth of Boston or Philadelphia?

options.text: New York was the only Atlantic port where foreign ships were allowed to dock and unload.
options.misconception: Foreign ships docked at Boston, Philadelphia, and other ports too; New York had no such monopoly.

options.text: Boston and Philadelphia had already built their own canals reaching the Great Lakes.
options.misconception: Neither Boston nor Philadelphia had a canal to the Great Lakes; that was exactly New York's edge.

options.text: The canal was dug entirely by enslaved laborers sent north by southern planters.
options.misconception: The canal was dug by paid laborers, many of them Irish immigrants, not by enslaved people.

options.text: The canal gave New York the only water route from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic.

rationales.A: Foreign ships docked at Boston, Philadelphia, and other Atlantic ports too. New York held no monopoly on foreign shipping.
rationales.B: Neither Boston nor Philadelphia had a canal reaching the Great Lakes. That missing link was exactly New York's edge.
rationales.C: The canal was dug by paid laborers, many of them Irish immigrants. Enslaved laborers were not sent north to dig it.
rationales.D: Before the canal, western goods reached the Atlantic through several rival ports. Background: once the canal opened in 1825, the cheapest water route ran through New York, and the city's trade and population surged past its rivals.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the rivals. Boston and Philadelphia were older, bigger ports than New York in 1800.
2. Look at the map the canal drew. One water road now ran from the Great Lakes straight to New York harbor.
3. Ask what shippers do. They take the cheapest route, so western grain and goods flowed through New York.
4. Put it together. The canal handed New York the West's trade, and the city pulled ahead for good.
Remember: a single cheap route can decide which city wins a region's trade.
